title: admin@338
summary: admin@338 is a cluster name for espionage activity that public reporting links to China-nexus operators and describes as targeting financial services, government, and media organisations, with an emphasis on Hong Kong and Southeast Asia. The reported technique set is shaped by the lure, not by advanced exploitation: emails that present an economic or political document, an attached file that requires the reader to enable active content, and a small downloader that retrieves a remote access family. Because the initial file is often benign until the reader grants permission, gateway scanning alone frequently misses it, and detection depends on endpoint telemetry showing document readers starting script hosts, debuggers, or signing utilities. Public documentation is relatively sparse and partly single-source, so claims about the group should be presented as reported rather than established. The common misunderstanding is that a campaign must be technically sophisticated to be dangerous. Here the discipline is patience, good lures, and reused tooling, which is often enough.

beginner.definition: admin@338 is a research label for a cyber spying group that public reports link to China. It goes after banks, government offices, and news organisations, mainly in Asia. It uses email files that ask the reader to switch on active content.
beginner.whyItMatters: Financial and media organisations hold private information that is valuable to spies. The harmful part of the attack starts only after the reader clicks allow, so scanners often pass the file. Staff in these sectors receive documents all day, which makes the trick believable. If endpoint logging is off, nobody sees the follow-up program. Detecting the file is not enough. You must detect the process it starts.
howItWorks: The attackers write a lure about money, policy, or politics to fit the reader.
They attach a document and send it to staff who already handle that topic.
The document looks blank or normal until the reader enables the active content.
Enabling it runs a small script, which then downloads a second program.
That second program gives the attackers full remote control of the workstation.
They then look for shared drives and collect the files that look valuable.
beginner.example: Think of a sealed letter that arrives with a note saying the important page is inside a locked sleeve. The envelope looks official and the topic is one you handle daily, so you open the sleeve as instructed. The sleeve is the trick. The letter itself was harmless, and only your action of opening it released what came next. Email documents with macros follow this pattern. The attachment passes every check because it stays harmless until a person grants permission. That permission is usually granted without a second thought.
takeaways: A harmless-looking attachment can become harmful after one click.
Watch what starts after a document opens, not only the file itself.
Turn on detailed endpoint logging so those follow-up steps are visible.

objectives: Explain why documents that require user permission often bypass attachment scanning.
Describe the delivery chain from lure document to remote access program.
Identify endpoint process relationships that indicate a malicious document ran.
Explain the value of financial, government, and media data to espionage operators.
Describe logging and alerting settings needed to detect this activity pattern.
Present sparse, partly single-source reporting about a group without overstating it.
